transcript.content: Hi, it’s good to meet you. What brings you in today?

I’m here because I can’t seem to keep my mind on the thing I’m actually supposed to be doing anymore, and it’s gotten… honestly, it’s gotten pretty serious at work. I’m a physical scientist, so a lot of what I do depends on sustained attention — experiments, meetings, grant calls, safety discussions, all the details that have to line up — and lately I’ll be in the middle of something important and my brain just veers off.

Like, during a grant call, someone will be talking about a deadline or what needs to be submitted, and I’ll suddenly notice some tiny thing — a pump vibration in the lab nearby, or some side comment a student makes, or I’ll remember an odd peak in an old spectrum — and then I’m gone. Not physically gone, but mentally I’m completely off chasing that thread. I’ll spend hours trying to figure out the vibration or digging through old data or following some tangent that feels urgent in the moment, and meanwhile the thing people actually needed from me just… falls apart.

It’s not just being a little distracted. It’s like everything grabs me at once, and the original task stops existing until there’s a problem. That’s why I came in. I can’t keep operating like this.
Have there been times when you felt unusually energized or high compared with your normal self?

Yes. I mean… yes, for months now I’ve felt almost like the lab is finally moving at my speed, if that makes sense. Like everything is lit up or electrified, and I’m not dragging myself through the day — I’m ahead of it. Ideas connect faster, problems look obvious, plans feel like they should happen immediately.

But it’s not just pleasant. It has this edge to it. If someone questions the plan, or even just asks me to slow down and explain, I can feel myself snap before I’ve really decided to. I’ll hear my voice get sharp, and I’ll think, why are they making this so difficult? And then afterward I realize I came down way too hard.

It’s gotten bad enough that some of the students seem to avoid my office now. They’ll email instead of coming in, or they hover at the door like they’re bracing for me to be irritated. That’s… embarrassing to say, because I don’t want to be that person. But yes, I’ve felt unusually energized, and also much more irritable when people don’t keep up with me.
During this period, have you been needing much less sleep than usual and still feeling rested?

Yes. Very much so. I used to need a normal night — not perfect, but at least something like seven hours if I was going to function. Lately it’s more like… two or three hours most nights, and somehow I wake up feeling sharp, not wrecked.

A lot of nights I don’t even properly go to bed. I’ll be on the couch with my laptop open, meaning to just check something or write down one idea, and then it’s 2 or 3 in the morning. I’ll doze off for a short stretch, sometimes with the laptop still there, and when I wake up I don’t feel like, “Oh no, I’m exhausted.” It’s more like I’m already switched on. Ready to get back to work.

Honestly, sleep has started to feel like this inefficient interruption, like something that gets in the way of the momentum. I know that probably sounds bad, but in the moment it doesn’t feel bad. It feels like I don’t need it.
Have you been taking on a lot more projects or activities than usual lately?

Yes — definitely. I’ve been taking on… honestly, a ridiculous amount, although in the moment it doesn’t feel ridiculous. It feels necessary.

I’m getting to the lab before anyone else is there, sometimes when the building still feels half-asleep, and I’ll already have a list going in my head. I start rewriting protocols because I suddenly see all these inefficiencies that seem obvious. Then I’ll jump to rearranging the instrument schedule because I’m convinced we can get three more runs in if people would just stop being so slow about it. Then I’m emailing collaborators in different time zones — Europe, Asia, wherever — because it feels like if I wait until normal hours, the whole thing loses momentum.

And I’m not doing one project at a time. That’s part of the problem. I’ll have new analyses open, old datasets pulled up, a draft protocol, scheduling emails, and some plan for a new experiment all happening at once. I keep telling myself I’m finally fixing things that have been stuck for years, but it’s like I can’t sit still long enough to finish one thing before another thing looks urgent.

It feels like sitting still is wasting the one chance to get everything into shape. Like if I don’t do it right now, all the pieces will scatter again.
During this energized period, have you had experiences like hearing or seeing things other people didn’t, or becoming convinced of something others said wasn’t true?

I don’t think so. I mean, not in the way you’re asking, I don’t think. I haven’t been seeing things in the room that other people say aren’t there, or hearing voices, if that’s what you mean.

The “convinced of something” part is harder, because I have been very, very sure of my own read on things lately — like sure that an approach is correct or that people are missing something obvious — but that feels more like intensity, not like… I don’t know, a belief that reality itself is different. If someone says, “That calculation is wrong,” I may argue too hard, but I’m not convinced the instruments are sending me messages or anything like that.

So, no, I haven’t noticed anything like hearing or seeing things others don’t. And if people disagree with me, it’s usually about work decisions or whether I’m moving too fast, not them saying something I believe is impossible or untrue.
Has this period caused serious problems at work or in your relationships?

Yes. I mean… I wanted to say no at first, because I keep thinking, “The work is still getting done,” or at least I’m working constantly, so it feels like that should count for something. But realistically, yes, it’s caused serious problems.

My department has had to step in on things I used to be trusted to handle myself. Decisions I normally would make — priorities for the project, who should be doing what, when certain lab activities should happen — people have started taking those out of my hands or checking them much more closely. And I hate saying that, because I’ve always been someone they could rely on. I’m not usually the person who creates confusion.

But lately I’ve been missing what actually needs attention first. I’ll be absolutely focused on one piece that seems urgent to me, and then something more basic or more important gets neglected or pushed around. The scheduling has gotten… tangled. I’ll move things or try to fit too much in, and then other people don’t know what’s actually happening, or equipment time gets confused, or staff are frustrated because I’ve changed direction again.

It’s also strained the way I supervise people. I can tell they’re walking on eggshells with me, or they’re irritated because I’m pushing too hard and not listening enough. And the part that scares me a little is that it got to the point where it wasn’t just interpersonal friction — the department was worried about the project and about whether lab safety expectations were being protected properly. Not that I was trying to be careless. I wasn’t. But the pace and the disorganization, or the way I was overriding normal checks, made people feel like they had to intervene.

So… yes. It’s not just annoying people. It has actually affected my role at work and their confidence in my judgment.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the elevated/irritable mood has caused marked functional impairment severe enough to support mania rather than hypomania.
doctor.question: Has this period caused serious problems at work or in your relationships?

target_item.name: Functional Impairment
target_item.manifestation: My department has had to step in on decisions I used to handle because missed priorities, confused scheduling, and strained supervision started putting the project and lab safety expectations at risk.
